title: The Foot Washing and the New Commandment
summary: At the evening meal before Passover, Jesus rises, takes a towel, and washes his disciples' feet, including Peter's after a protest, and tells them to follow his example. He announces that one of them will betray him, gives the morsel to Judas, and Judas goes out into the night. Jesus then gives the disciples a new commandment to love one another as he has loved them, and warns Peter that he will deny him three times.
story: With chapter 13 the second half of John's Gospel begins. Jesus' public ministry is over, and for five chapters (13 to 17) the reader is inside a single room on a single night, listening as Jesus prepares his closest followers for his departure. This long section is often called the Upper Room Discourse or the Farewell Discourse. The chapter's first verse sets the tone for everything that follows: Jesus knew his hour had come, and “He loved them to the very end.” The foot washing shows that love in action, and the rest of the discourse will explain it. Judas's departure and Peter's coming denial show that the love is given to disciples who will fail.
historical:
John dates this meal “just before the Passover Feast” (13:1), and later says the authorities would not enter Pilate's headquarters so that they could eat the Passover (18:28) and that Jesus was crucified on the day of Preparation (19:14). In Matthew, Mark, and Luke the Last Supper appears to be the Passover meal itself. How these accounts relate is a long-standing question, taken up below under the hard question.

The beloved disciple appears here for the first time by that description, reclining next to Jesus (13:23). The Gospel later identifies him as the source of its testimony (21:24) but never names him. Church tradition since the second century has identified him as John the son of Zebedee, one of the Twelve. Some modern scholars suggest another follower, such as Lazarus, whom Jesus is said to love (11:3, 5), or a disciple based in Jerusalem who was not one of the Twelve. Judas Iscariot is identified as the son of Simon Iscariot; the name Iscariot is often explained as man of Kerioth, a town in Judea, though other explanations have been offered.
cultural:
At a formal meal guests reclined on couches or cushions around a low table, leaning on the left elbow with their feet stretched out behind them. That arrangement explains how the beloved disciple could lean back against Jesus (13:25) and how Jesus could reach the disciples' feet. People walked dusty roads in sandals, and washing a guest's feet on arrival was a courtesy, usually done by the lowest household servant, or the guest was given water to do it himself. For a teacher to wash his students' feet was unheard of, and for a host to strip to a servant's towel was humiliating, which explains Peter's horror.

Sharing bread with someone was a bond of friendship, so betrayal by one who shared a meal was especially bitter; Jesus cites Psalm 41:9, “The one who shares My bread has lifted up his heel against Me” (13:18). Giving a dipped morsel to a guest could be a gesture of honor. Jesus offers it to Judas even as he identifies him as the betrayer.
literary: The chapter moves from action to meaning. The foot washing (13:1-11) is an acted parable, and Jesus explains it twice: first to Peter as a cleansing without which he has no part with Jesus, then to all as an example of humble service (13:12-17). The account of the betrayal (13:18-30) ends with one of the most loaded short sentences in the Gospel: Judas “went out into the night” (13:30). In John night is more than a time; it is the darkness that the light has come to overcome. The last section (13:31-38) opens the discourse proper with the announcement of glory, the new commandment, and the warning to Peter. John's verbs in 13:4 (he laid aside his garments) and 13:12 (he put them on again) echo the language of the shepherd who lays down his life and takes it up again (10:17-18), so the scene quietly points to the cross.

outline.t: Jesus foretells the betrayal; Judas goes out

doctrines.note: “By this everyone will know that you are My disciples, if you love one another” (13:35). The mark of Jesus' community is not first its doctrine or its success but its love, measured by his: “As I have loved you, so you also must love one another” (13:34).

“Unless I wash you, you have no part with Me” (13:8). The foot washing pictures the cleansing that only Jesus can give. The one who has bathed needs only to wash his feet (13:10), which many readers take to mean that those made clean through Christ still need ongoing cleansing from daily sin.

Some Christian traditions, including several Anabaptist and Baptist groups and Seventh-day Adventists, practice foot washing as an ordinance because of 13:14-15. Many churches keep it as a rite on the Thursday before Easter, and most treat it as an example of humble service rather than a sacrament. This is a second-order difference among faithful churches.

words.note: Niptō, to wash part of the body, such as the hands or feet. In 13:10 John sets it beside louō, to bathe the whole body: the one who has bathed needs only to wash his feet. The distinction matters to Jesus' reply to Peter, who asks to be washed all over.

Hupodeigma, example or pattern. Jesus says, “I have set you an example” (13:15). The word means a model to be copied, not merely an illustration. The disciples are to reproduce his humility in their own service.

Kainos, new. The command to love one's neighbor was old (Leviticus 19:18). What is new is its measure and source, as Jesus has loved them, and the new community it creates. Kainos often carries the sense of fresh or of a new kind, and it links this command to the new covenant.

Agapaō, to love. It appears six times in the chapter, which opens with Jesus loving his own to the end (13:1) and closes with the command to love as he loved. In John the verb describes the Father's love for the Son, the Son's love for the disciples, and the love they are to show each other.

christ: In washing feet, Jesus acts out what Paul would later describe in Philippians 2: the one who was in the form of God took the form of a servant and humbled himself to death on a cross. John tells us Jesus did this knowing that the Father had put all things into his hands and that he came from God and was going to God (13:3). His humility is not a lack of status but the use of supreme status for others. The foot washing points to the cross, the greater cleansing without which no one has a part with him. And by telling the disciples of the betrayal in advance, “so that when it comes to pass, you will believe that I am He” (13:19), Jesus shows that he goes to his death knowingly, as the one who bears God's name.

hard.q: Was the Last Supper a Passover meal, as the other Gospels suggest, or did it happen the day before, as John seems to say?
hard.a:
Matthew, Mark, and Luke describe the Last Supper as a Passover meal (Mark 14:12-16), while John places the crucifixion on the day of Preparation, when the Passover lambs were being slaughtered (19:14; 18:28). Scholars have offered several explanations. Some think John changed the date to present Jesus as the Passover lamb; others think the Synoptic Gospels turned a farewell meal into a Passover meal. Some harmonizing proposals argue that different Jewish groups followed different calendars in this period, so that Jesus and his disciples kept Passover a day earlier than the temple authorities (a view developed by the French scholar Annie Jaubert). Others argue that John's references to the Passover in 18:28 and the day of Preparation in 19:14 can refer to the whole week-long festival and the day before the Sabbath, so that the accounts agree after all. Still others suggest Jesus held a Passover-style meal a day early, knowing he would die before the feast.

None of these proposals has settled the question. What all the Gospels agree on is that Jesus died at Passover, in the context of Israel's great feast of deliverance, and that his death was the fulfillment of what it signified.

questions: Peter first refuses to let Jesus wash his feet. Why can it be harder to receive humble love than to give it?
Jesus washed Judas's feet too. What does that suggest about how far his example of service is meant to reach?
If people judged Jesus' followers only by their love for one another, what would they conclude about your church?
